column1: What founding invariant did NFSv2 embrace regarding server-side client context?
column2: Complete statelessness—the server maintains zero per-client context; every request is a self-contained transaction carrying a file handle and all parameters needed for atomic execution.

column1: Why does complete statelessness in NFSv2 prevent byte-range locking and write deferral optimizations?
column2: Because the server never tracks which files clients have opened, it cannot coordinate exclusive access or safely delay writes for disk scheduling optimization.

column1: What three components does the default Linux nfsd file handle encoding pack together?
column2: A filesystem UUID, an inode number, and a generation counter.

column1: Why does the inode generation counter matter for file handle correctness after deletion/recreation?
column2: When a file is deleted and a new file reuses the same inode number, the generation counter increments, so stale handles trigger NFS3ERR_STALE instead of silently accessing the wrong data.

column1: What are the three NFSv4 filehandle types and their validity guarantees?
column2: Persistent (must remain valid across server restarts), volatile (may become invalid, flagged accordingly), and anonymous (used only for initial PUTROOTFH/PUTPUBFH operations).

column1: Why do most production NFS servers advertise persistent filehandles rather than volatile ones?
column2: Because volatile handles would require clients to re-traverse the entire directory tree after a server reboot, which is operationally catastrophic at scale.

column1: What is the NFS client file handle opacity invariant?
column2: The client neither parses nor constructs file handles; it only stores and caches them, treating them as opaque tokens minted entirely by the server.

column1: What consistency model does NFS implement for caching, and what does it guarantee?
column2: Close-to-open consistency: changes made by one client become visible to another when files are explicitly closed and reopened; no guarantee exists for concurrent readers observing writes before synchronization boundaries.

column1: What three distinct layers does NFS client-side caching operate across?
column2: Data blocks (page cache), metadata attributes (attribute cache), and directory entries (DNLC - Directory Name Lookup Cache).

column1: What is the validation-on-timeout protocol for NFS cached attributes?
column2: When a cache timeout expires, the client issues a GETATTR RPC and compares returned mtime/ctime against cached values; a mismatch forces discarding stale cached data and refetching from the server.

column1: What is the core security weakness of AUTH_SYS (AUTH_UNIX) authentication in NFS?
column2: It transmits numeric UID/GID in cleartext within RPC headers without cryptographic proof, relying entirely on network perimeter security—allowing any attacker with network access to forge arbitrary UIDs.

column1: How does RPCSEC_GSS (via Kerberos v5) improve on AUTH_SYS, and what does it establish?
column2: It introduces cryptographic challenge-response authentication via a trusted KDC issuing time-limited tickets, establishing mutual authentication and enabling per-RPC integrity (MACs) or confidentiality (encryption).
